cited_details.statement: Automotive millimeter-wave radar has become a foundational sensor for autonomous driving because of its weather robustness, low cost, and ability to directly measure target velocity through the Doppler effect [https://doi.org/10.3390/s20247283].

With the maturation of deep learning, radar signal processing has progressively shifted from classical detection pipelines toward learned representations that are explicitly designed for neural networks [https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.09304].

This transformation has produced a diverse taxonomy of radar data representations, each encoding trade-offs between information density, computational cost, and compatibility with downstream perception tasks [https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.09304].

Conventional automotive radar typically produces a 3D Radar Tensor (3DRT) that stores power values along the Doppler, range, and azimuth axes [https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/hash/185fdf627eaae2abab36205dcd19b817-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.html].

Because 3DRT lacks an elevation component, reliably estimating 3D bounding boxes for objects is difficult [https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/hash/185fdf627eaae2abab36205dcd19b817-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.html].

Next-generation 4D imaging radars address this limitation by emitting a 4D Radar Tensor (4DRT) that adds an elevation dimension and produces substantially denser, spatially richer measurements [https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/hash/185fdf627eaae2abab36205dcd19b817-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.html].

The KAIST-Radar (K-Radar) dataset was introduced to support deep learning research on 4DRT, providing 35K frames captured under diverse weather conditions [https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/hash/185fdf627eaae2abab36205dcd19b817-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.html].

Beyond the static power tensor, raw radio-frequency radar tensors retain spatiotemporal semantics that are typically discarded by constant-false-alarm-rate detectors but can be exploited for joint detection and tracking [https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.01423].

A parallel research direction operates directly on the complex-valued baseband samples emitted by the radar front end, avoiding the information loss caused by intermediate envelope detection [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.12187].

The Deep Radar Detector demonstrated that a convolutional network trained on calibration data can perform 4D detection while consuming the complex radar data, removing dependence on hand-engineered features [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.12187].

In the Range-Doppler domain specifically, deep networks have been shown to improve target detection over classical two-dimensional FFT plus thresholding pipelines [http://vigir.ee.missouri.edu/~gdesouza/Research/Conference_CDs/IEEE_WCCI_2020/IJCNN/Papers/N-21054.pdf].
Because radar natively acquires measurements in a polar coordinate system, learning directly in the polar domain has emerged as a natural design choice [https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.03387].

PolarNet reformulates the radar tensor as a polar bird's-eye-view grid, exploiting the radial geometry of the sensor to accelerate free-space segmentation without sacrificing angular resolution [https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.03387].

Production automotive radar stacks traditionally output sparse point clouds in Cartesian coordinates, and these points have long served as the dominant interface to downstream perception modules [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9185239/].
However, projecting sparse radar points onto the image plane yields very sparse depth maps that are difficult to consume directly in camera-based pipelines [https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02720].

To address this, learning-based upsampling has been proposed to densify radar point clouds prior to fusion, producing more useful geometric features for downstream depth estimation [https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02720].

Because radar returns are inherently noisy and difficult to label at scale, cross-modal supervision from cameras has become a leading representation-learning paradigm [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ISTSP..15..954W/abstract].

RODNet introduced a real-time radar object detection network whose training signal is derived from a camera-radar fusion algorithm, allowing it to operate on range-angle-Doppler radar tensors without manually annotated radar labels [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ISTSP..15..954W/abstract].

This line of work was subsequently extended with a 3D variant and the CRUW3D dataset containing 66K synchronized camera, radar, and LiDAR frames for diverse driving scenarios [https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/RODNet%3A-Radar-Object-Detection-using-Cross-Modal-Wang-Jiang/3b858058c04da3871848b81e8d8304e24c1282d5].

In parallel, self-supervised learning has been investigated to bootstrap rich radar feature representations without any manual labels, directly tackling the chronic shortage of annotated radar data [https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04519].
A growing body of work fuses radar with cameras in the feature space rather than at the output level, leading to a new class of joint representations [https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.07825].

Representation learning for radar-camera fusion has been demonstrated to exploit the complementary physical properties of the two sensors while remaining compatible with mass-production automotive hardware [https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.07825].

More recently, a modality-interaction architecture incorporating radar Gaussian splatting has been proposed to further sharpen 3D object detection by aligning the two sensor streams [https://spj.science.org/doi/pdf/10.34133/cbsystems.0079].
A complementary direction compresses the high-dimensional 3D radar signal into compact 2D planes to enable efficient segmentation under tight latency constraints [https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.12940].

The ERASE-Net family replaces the 3D input with carefully chosen 2D projections while attempting to retain the information required for accurate free-space segmentation [https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.12940].

The field has progressed from hand-crafted radar signal processing toward a rich palette of learned representations spanning complex data, 3D and 4D tensors, polar grids, point clouds, cross-modal embeddings, and self-supervised features [https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.09304].

Continued advances in 4D imaging radar hardware, large-scale annotated datasets, and self-supervised pre-training are expected to further close the performance gap between radar and camera- or LiDAR-based perception in safety-critical driving scenarios [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9185239/].

evidence.title: PolarNet: Accelerated Deep Open Space Segmentation Using Automotive Radar in Polar Domain
evidence.abstract: Camera and Lidar processing have been revolutionized with the rapid development of deep learning model architectures. Automotive radar is one of the crucial elements of automated driver assistance and autonomous driving systems. Radar still relies on traditional signal processing techniques, unlike camera and Lidar based methods. We believe this is the missing link to achieve the most robust perception system. Identifying drivable space and occupied space is the first step in any autonomous decision making task. Occupancy grid map representation of the environment is often used for this purpose. In this paper, we propose PolarNet, a deep neural model to process radar information in polar domain for open space segmentation. We explore various input-output representations. Our experiments show that PolarNet is a effective way to process radar data that achieves state-of-the-art performance and processing speeds while maintaining a compact size.

evidence.title: MMW Radar-Based Technologies in Autonomous Driving: A Review
evidence.abstract: With the rapid development of automated vehicles (AVs), more and more demands are proposed towards environmental perception. Among the commonly used sensors, MMW radar plays an important role due to its low cost, adaptability In different weather, and motion detection capability. Radar can provide different data types to satisfy requirements for various levels of autonomous driving. The objective of this study is to present an overview of the state-of-the-art radar-based technologies applied In AVs. Although several published research papers focus on MMW Radars for intelligent vehicles, no general survey on deep learning applied In radar data for autonomous vehicles exists. Therefore, we try to provide related survey In this paper. First, we introduce models and representations from millimeter-wave (MMW) radar data. Secondly, we present radar-based applications used on AVs. For low-level automated driving, radar data have been widely used In advanced driving-assistance systems (ADAS). For high-level automated driving, radar data is used In object detection, object tracking, motion prediction, and self-localization. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges and future development direction of related studies.

evidence.title: Radar Camera Fusion via Representation Learning in Autonomous Driving
evidence.abstract: Radars and cameras are mature, cost-effective, and robust sensors and have been widely used in the perception stack of mass-produced autonomous driving systems. Due to their complementary properties, outputs from radar detection (radar pins) and camera perception (2D bounding boxes) are usually fused to generate the best perception results. The key to successful radar-camera fusion is the accurate data association. The challenges in the radar-camera association can be attributed to the complexity of driving scenes, the noisy and sparse nature of radar measurements, and the depth ambiguity from 2D bounding boxes. Traditional rule-based association methods are susceptible to performance degradation in challenging scenarios and failure in corner cases. In this study, we propose to address radar-camera association via deep representation learning, to explore feature-level interaction and global reasoning. Additionally, we design a loss sampling mechanism and an innovative ordinal loss to overcome the difficulty of imperfect labeling and to enforce critical human-like reasoning. Despite being trained with noisy labels generated by a rule-based algorithm, our proposed method achieves a performance of 92.2% F1 score, which is 11.6% higher than the rule-based teacher. Moreover, this data-driven method also lends itself to continuous improvement via corner case mining.
